whyItExists.problem: Databases are slow compared to Redis. Without caching, every API request hits the database, causing high latency and load. But naive caching leads to stale data, thundering herds, and inconsistency.
whyItExists.solution: Cache patterns define a contract between the application, cache, and database. Each pattern makes a different tradeoff between consistency, simplicity, and performance.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any time you have read-heavy workloads with data that is expensive to compute or fetch and can tolerate slight staleness.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Financial transactions, inventory counts, or any data that must always be fresh — or when cache misses would actually be more expensive than just reading from the DB.

explainModes.beginner: Caching is like keeping a cheat sheet. Instead of recalculating everything from scratch, you write the answer down. Cache-aside means the app fills the cheat sheet on demand. Write-through means you update the cheat sheet every time you change the original.
explainModes.simple: Cache-aside: app checks cache, misses → load DB → write cache. Write-through: every DB write also writes cache. Write-behind: write cache immediately, write DB later in bulk. Read-through: cache fetches from DB itself.
explainModes.standard: Cache-aside (lazy loading) is the most flexible: the application manages cache population on cache misses. Write-through keeps cache consistent with every write. Write-behind (write-back) improves write performance by deferring DB writes. Read-through hides cache logic inside a middleware layer.
explainModes.technical: Cache-aside has eventual consistency between cache and DB during TTL window. Write-through has stronger consistency but doubles write latency. Write-behind risks data loss on cache failure before DB flush. Cache stampede (thundering herd) occurs when many concurrent misses all hit the DB; prevent with mutex (SETNX lock) or probabilistic early expiry.
explainModes.deepDive: Probabilistic early expiry: instead of expiring at TTL, expire with probability p = exp(-β * t_remaining) as the key approaches expiry. The first cache client to 'early-expire' recomputes while others still serve the old value, eliminating the stampede. The XFetch algorithm implements this. For high-read caches, consider hot-key replication: write the same value to key:0 through key:9 and read from a random shard.

content.text: The most common pattern. The application is responsible for populating the cache: check Redis first, fetch from the DB on a miss, and store the result in Redis for future requests.

content.definition: When the requested data is not in the cache and must be fetched from the original source (database, API, or computed). A miss triggers cache population.

content.text: Every write to the database also writes to the cache synchronously. The cache is always up to date, but writes are slower (two writes instead of one).
Instead of write-through, some patterns simply invalidate (delete) the cached entry on update. The next read will trigger a fresh cache-aside fetch.
When a popular cache entry expires, hundreds of requests simultaneously miss and all hit the database at once. This is a cache stampede (thundering herd). Prevent it with a distributed lock.

a.name: Cache-Aside
strengths: Only caches data that is actually read
DB failure on write doesn't corrupt cache
weaknesses: Cache is stale until TTL expires or invalidated
First request after expiry is slow (miss)
a.useWhen: Most read-heavy applications with tolerable brief staleness

b.name: Write-Through
strengths: Cache is always up to date
weaknesses: Caches data that may never be read (write waste)
Cache and DB must succeed atomically
b.useWhen: When data consistency is critical and write latency is acceptable

content.text: Always set a TTL on cached values. Without a TTL, stale data lives forever and memory fills up. A TTL of 5 minutes is a safe default for most application caches.

questions.question: In cache-aside, who is responsible for populating the cache?
questions.explanation: In cache-aside, the application populates the cache when a miss occurs. The cache never talks to the database directly.

questions.question: What is a cache stampede?
options: When Redis runs out of memory
When many concurrent requests all miss the cache and hit the database simultaneously
When cache keys have no TTL
When the write-through pattern is used
questions.explanation: A cache stampede (thundering herd) happens when a popular key expires and many concurrent requests all go to the database at once before any can re-populate the cache.

questions.question: What is the main disadvantage of write-through caching?
options: Every write has double latency (DB + cache)
questions.explanation: Write-through writes to both the cache and database on every mutation, increasing write latency. It trades write performance for read consistency.

faq.a: When many requests all miss the cache simultaneously and all hit the database at once. Prevent with a distributed mutex (SETNX), probabilistic early expiry, or background refresh.

faq.q: How do I handle cache aside when the DB query is expensive?
faq.a: Use a distributed lock (SETNX) so only one request recomputes while others wait. This is the 'read-through with locking' pattern.
Yes — cache a sentinel value (e.g. empty string or 'NULL') with a short TTL to prevent repeated DB hits for non-existent entities. This is called 'negative caching'.

examples: Caching product details for 5 minutes reduced PostgreSQL CPU by 70%
Cache-aside with stampede lock prevented DB overload during traffic spikes
